newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish shares slump on inflation, political worry.
newsitem.headline: Turkish shares slump on inflation, political worry.

text.p: Concern about the future of Turkey's Islamist-led coalition and higher-than-expected inflation sent Turkish shares tumbling nine percent on Tuesday morning, analysts and brokers said.
The IMKB National-100 index ended the morning session down 137 points, or 9.0 percent at 1,385. Trading volume rose to 12.49 trillion lira ($101 million) from 9.54 trillion on Monday morning.

The release of February inflation data accelerated a bout of selling fuelled by anticipation of a government censure motion debate and newspaper reports indicating Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller's party may consider pulling out of the coalition.
"A situation where the government could fall at any moment has put the market under considerable pressure and pulled it lower," said Mustafa Karaahmetoglu of Sayilgan Securities.

Dealers said the decline, adding to a 5.6 percent fall on Monday, had nearly bottomed-out. Karaahmetoglu said prices were attractive at current levels, despite concerns about the leading opposition party's censure motion to be debated in parliament later in the day.
"Tension over the censure motion influences the market negatively. But the index is not going to see below 1,350 points," said Koray Cervatoglu of Baran Securities.
The sudden trend reversal followed a period of market optimism about the eight-month-old government's ability to revive a flagging privatisation programme and push ahead with structural reforms.
Shares leapt 65 percent in the first two months of the year on hopes that political stability would provide a basis for stabilising an economy beleaguered by annual inflation of around 80 percent.

On Tuesday, the State Institute of Statistics said February wholesale prices rose 6.2 percent on the month and an annual 78.6 percent. Consumer prices were up a monthly 5.7 percent and 77.7 percent annually.
The figures further upset market sentiment after forecasts of 4.5-5.5 percent month-on-month inflation had boosted demand for dollars, prompting Turkish central bank intervention.

The central bank sold dollars for lira and the dollar fell to 123,600 lira level after the intervention which began at around 123,770 lira. T-bill and bond yields jumped as much as seven percentage points to around 102 percent following the price data.

Confidence in the government's ability to address the economy's deep-seated problems has been eroded by a warning from military leaders about the direction Turkey was taking under its first Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan.

The military-dominated National Security Council issued a set of demands last Friday aimed at reversing recent Islamist zeal partly encouraged by Erbakan's Welfare Party. The warning has cast doubt in the market about the future of the government.
According to Global Securities research director Atilla Yesilada, the Welfare Party could either conform to the army's wishes and risk losing its core support, or the government could split.
"I think the government splitting soon is more likely as I do not see how Welfare could explain this to its constituency," he said.

Speculation about the future of the alliance was heightened by newspaper reports that True Path Party (DYP) leader Ciller would pull out of the alliance if Erbakan did not try to stamp out Islamist activism soon.
"We are not locked into the government. We will pull out if the conditions require it," the Milliyet newspaper quoted conservative Ciller as telling her DYP aides on Monday.
